To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in the fasting state, the liver takes up LDL cholesterol and secretes it into bile; in the fed state, the liver secretes LDL cholesterol and VLDL cholesterol into bile and takes up LDL cholesterol from plasma.
LDL cholesterol uptake by the fasting baboon liver is appreciable, contributing to biliary sterols.

LDL cholesterol uptake by the splanchnic bed in baboons is appreciable, that LDL cholesterol uptake is the main determinant of biliary sterol flux, and that HDL cholesterol uptake or secretion by the liver or the splanchnics cannot be detected by trans-gradient analysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a primate model of net hepatic flux of lipoprotein sterol, and with the application of this model to the study of the regulation of biliary sterol excretion in normal and pathological states.
the study of cholesterol metabolism and transport in the primate model.
the development of a primate model that allows the study of hepatoenteric cholesterol metabolism in conscious, healthy fed or fasting primates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in the fasting baboons LDL cholesterol uptake is appreciable and is a major source of cholesterol transferred to bile.

lipoprotein cholesterol uptake and/or secretion by the liver or intestine cannot be detected by trans-gradient analysis, but in the tracer studies appears to be a major route for transfer of cholesterol to bile in the fasted baboon.
the liver in the baboon, as in the human, is a site of net lipoprotein cholesterol uptake in the fasted state and net lipoprotein secretion in the fed state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

in the fasting baboons LDL cholesterol was the major cholesterol source to the liver and to the bile, whereas in the fed state the major source to the liver was LDL cholesterol and to the bile was HDL cholesterol.
the liver is an important site for LDL cholesterol uptake in both the fasting and the fed state, whereas HDL cholesterol is an important source of biliary sterol in the fed state.
net cholesterol fluxes by the splanchnic bed, the portal region, and the liver are all important in the regulation of biliary cholesterol secretion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LDL cholesterol is taken up by the liver in the fasting state and is a major source of biliary cholesterol in the fasting state in the baboon.
the liver is a significant site of cholesterol uptake from plasma LDL, which in turn contributes to biliary cholesterol secretion in the fasting state.
LDL cholesterol uptake by the primate liver is a major contributor to biliary cholesterol secretion, whereas HDL cholesterol uptake or secretion is a major contributor only in the fed state.
